newsitem.title: USA: Congress moves to stop reverse mortgage scams.
newsitem.headline: Congress moves to stop reverse mortgage scams.

text.p: U.S. lawmakers introduced legislation on Thursday to stop reverse mortgage scams that have bilked elderly homeowners of millions of dollars.

Telemarketers have preyed on the elderly by charging fees to provide information available for free from the federal government on reverse mortgages -- loans to homeowners that are not repaid until the owner dies or moves out of the house.
"Excessive reverse mortgage servicing fees are gouging low-income seniors," said Senate Banking Committee Chairman Alfonse D'Amato, who is sponsoring one of the bills. "That is just plain wrong."

The bills will "help rid these unconscionable practices and maintain a valuable instrument of security for our nation's senior homeowners," said Rep Rick Lazio, Republican of New York and House sponsor of the legislation.
Housing Secretary Andrew Cuomo, who had moved to curtail the scams at the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), welcomed the legislation.

Cuomo's effort to crack down on the scams -- limiting HUD reverse mortgage insurance on loans arranged by so-called estate-planning services -- was blocked last month by a temporary restraining order from a federal judge in Washington.
"We must act as quickly as possible, to prevent any more senior citizens from being victimized," Cuomo said.
In a typical transaction, a telemarketer might charge a homeowner a fee of eight to 10 percent of the amount of the reverse mortgage loan, or $5,000 to $10,000, the lawmakers said.
The legislation would make permanent the HUD policy barring lender dealings with companies charging "exorbitant fees," the lawmakers said.
